document_check.note: Egas-López JV, Balogh R, Imre N, et al. Automatic screening of mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s disease by means of posterior-thresholding hesitation representation. Computer Speech & Language 75 (2022) 101377. The paper is a Szeged Memory Clinic speech study (25 HC, 25 MCI, 25 mild AD) using pause and hesitation features. This matches the citation 'Egas-López et al. 2022'.

cited_result: Pause/hesitation (silent and filled pause) features as discriminative signals: three-class HC/MCI/mild AD classification with posterior-thresholding hesitation features (context-dependent DNN, all three speech tasks and feature sets fused), mean AUC 0.804 and MCI-class AUC 0.709. This is the principal result; the review cites the study only generically.
tool_reason: The cited result is the discriminative performance of an SVM classifier distinguishing MCI (and mild AD) from controls using speech pause features, which is a diagnostic machine-learning model question for PROBAST with PROBAST+AI considerations.

domains.rationale: From a corpus of more than 150 subjects, the authors removed those with poor sound quality or no diagnostic consensus, then selected demographically matched groups of 25 each. This artificial, balanced selection excludes the ambiguous cases a screening tool would meet, which inflates separability.

signalling.question: 1.1 Were appropriate data sources used?
signalling.quote: This corpus comprises recordings taken from more than 150 subjects. Due to technical issues like poor sound quality and controversial diagnosis (i.e. when our clinical expert panel could not reach a consensus), some subjects were filtered out.

signalling.question: 1.2 Were all inclusions and exclusions of participants appropriate?
signalling.quote: Furthermore, we insisted on performing our experiments on data where the demographic properties of the speaker groups did not differ significantly, which also reduced the number of subjects.

domains.rationale: Every participant followed the same three-task recording protocol. Features are computed automatically from the frame-level posteriors of a DNN acoustic model trained on an external corpus (BEA), and would be available at the time of use. Recordings were trimmed manually at the start and end only.

signalling.question: 2.1 Were predictors defined and assessed in a similar way for all participants?
signalling.quote: Hence, we had three recordings for each subject, each containing spontaneous speech with a different speaker task

signalling.question: 2.2 Were predictor assessments made without knowledge of outcome data?
signalling.quote: Each recording was edited; namely, parts before the subject started to speak and after his last phoneme uttered were manually removed.

signalling.question: 2.3 Are all predictors available at the time the model is intended to be used?
signalling.quote: Our Deep Neural Network acoustic models were trained on a subset of the BEA Hungarian corpus (Neuberger et al., 2014)

domains.rationale: MCI and mild AD were diagnosed by a multidisciplinary consensus panel using Petersen and McKhann criteria, independently of the speech features and before recording. Two details are not reported: how healthy controls were confirmed, and the interval between diagnosis and recording.

signalling.question: 3.1 Was the outcome determined appropriately?
signalling.quote: Diagnosis was based on the consensus of a clinical expert panel consisting of a psychiatrist, a neurologist and a psychologist, who reviewed neuroimaging scans (CT, MRI) when available, and also the results of three cognitive screenings tests

signalling.question: 3.2 Was a pre-specified or standard outcome definition used?
signalling.quote: In the case of MCI, Petersen’s criteria (Petersen et al., 1999), while for AD, internationally used guidelines (McKhann et al., 2011) were followed.

signalling.question: 3.3 Were predictors excluded from the outcome definition?
signalling.quote: who reviewed neuroimaging scans (CT, MRI) when available, and also the results of three cognitive screenings tests

signalling.question: 3.4 Was the outcome defined and determined in a similar way for all participants?
signalling.quote: those having no cognitive impairment at the time of recording (i.e. healthy controls, HC)

signalling.question: 3.5 Was the outcome determined without knowledge of predictor information?
signalling.quote: MCI and mAD patients were selected after a medical diagnosis.

signalling.question: 3.6 Was the time interval between predictor assessment and outcome determination appropriate?
signalling.quote: Searched Section 2 for the time between clinical diagnosis and speech recording; not reported.

domains.rationale: There are 25 participants per class against 51 to 151 features per recording, fused across three tasks. More than half the corpus was dropped, including subjects with poor sound quality (a complete-case approach). Performance is reported at the Equal Error Rate threshold with no calibration. The weights for fusing predictions are not described, and many configurations were compared, with the best reported in the abstract. Validation is internal only, although the hyperparameters were tuned by nested CV at the subject level.

applicability.rationale: The groups are artificially balanced and demographically matched (25/25/25), with contested diagnoses removed.
The primary task is three-class (HC/MCI/mild AD), and the headline binary metrics pool MCI with mild AD, so they do not directly answer MCI versus control.

overall_rationale: Domain 1 (selection of a matched 75-subject subset from more than 150, excluding contested diagnoses) and domain 4 (small sample against many features, many configurations with the best reported, undescribed fusion weights, EER-threshold metrics, no calibration, no external validation) are high.
